bottleneck: The glymphatic system — brain-wide cerebrospinal fluid flow clearing metabolic waste during sleep — is well demonstrated in mice but barely measurable in living humans. Whether impaired clearance causes Alzheimer's or merely accompanies it is unknown, because the system cannot be quantified longitudinally in people. No method exists to therapeutically enhance human glymphatic flow even if it proved causal, and the sleep-dependence of clearance means the mechanism is entangled with the equally mysterious function of sleep itself. A potentially central mechanism of brain aging is thus untestable in the species that matters.
current_state: MRI tracer studies show fluid movement in human brains, but causal links to disease remain speculative and no glymphatic-targeted intervention exists or is in trials.

title: Human glymphatic clearance unmeasurable in vivo
why_it_blocks: If the brain's waste-disposal system fails with aging, fixing it could prevent dementia before plaques ever form. But an unmeasurable system cannot be drugged, monitored, or even confirmed as a target.
